events.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
events.label: Dartmouth workshop
events.problem: Work on thinking machines was scattered across cybernetics, logic, information theory and early computing, with no shared name or agenda.
events.idea: In Aug 1955, McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon proposed a two-month summer study in 1956. Their conjecture was that every feature of learning or intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. The proposal coined 'artificial intelligence'.
events.changed: The workshop gave the field its name, founding community and early optimism. Its listed topics (language use, abstraction, self-improvement, neuron nets) remain on the research agenda.
events.limits: The workshop itself produced few concrete results, and its time estimates were far too optimistic. Early AI after Dartmouth was mostly symbolic, not learning-based.

links.note: the learning-machine strand that ran alongside symbolic AI

verified.note: Proposal PDF opened: dated 31 Aug 1955, study planned for summer 1956. Exact workshop dates not given on the Dartmouth page, so year precision.

events.date_context: 1958 Psychological Review paper; this is a journal milestone, not an arXiv submission.
events.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron
events.label: Perceptron
events.problem: It was unclear whether a machine could learn to classify patterns from examples rather than being programmed with rules.
events.idea: Rosenblatt described the perceptron, a network of threshold units whose weights are adjusted by an error-driven rule. The rule has a convergence guarantee for linearly separable data. The design was later built in hardware (Mark I).
events.changed: The perceptron brought trainable neural classifiers to wide attention and helped establish learning by adjusting weights as an alternative to programming every rule.
events.limits: A single layer of trainable weights can only learn linearly separable functions, and there was no method for training hidden layers. Press coverage greatly overstated what it could do.

links.note: the target of Minsky and Papert's analysis

terms.def: A linear classifier with a threshold output whose weights are updated only when it misclassifies an example.

verified.note: Crossref metadata: Psychological Review, 1958. Journal publication, not arXiv; date_basis field reused. doi.org blocks scripted requests (403) but the DOI is registered. Review 2026-11-06: Corrected mislabeled date_basis to journal publication. The original check used Crossref metadata; the DOI fetch itself was blocked.

events.date_context: 1969 original edition, confirmed by its publisher record; the expanded edition appeared in 1987. The book's causal role in the funding downturn remains disputed.
events.title: Minsky and Papert, Perceptrons, and the AI winters
events.label: Perceptrons and AI winters
events.problem: Claims about neural networks outpaced the theory of what they could compute.
events.idea: Minsky and Papert proved that single-layer perceptrons cannot compute some simple predicates (parity, connectedness; XOR is the textbook case) without impractically large or global connections.
events.changed: The book documented limitations of restricted perceptron architectures. It became associated with the first AI winter, alongside unmet promises and the UK Lighthill report (written in 1972, published in 1973); its independent role in funding cuts is disputed. A second downturn followed the expert-systems market contraction in the late 1980s.
events.limits: The results applied to single-layer networks. They did not rule out multilayer networks, but researchers could not yet train those. How much the book alone caused the downturn is disputed.

sources.label: Lighthill report, Part I (Chilton Computing archive)

links.note: backprop supplied a method for training hidden layers

terms.def: A period of reduced funding and interest in AI after promises outran results, notably the mid-1970s and late 1980s to early 1990s.

verified.note: MIT Press page (opened in browser) is the 1987 expanded edition; original 1969 edition is standard. Lighthill archive page dates the report July 1972; publication by the SRC was 1973. Review 2026-11-06: original-edition MIT Press record (ISBN 9780262130431) opened; it gives 15 Jan 1969. The expanded-edition page gives 28 Dec 1987. Retained year precision for the historical milestone.

events.date_context: October 1986 Nature paper; reverse-mode differentiation and earlier neural-network applications predate this milestone.
events.title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors
events.label: Backpropagation popularised
events.problem: Multilayer networks could represent much more than perceptrons, but there was no widely accepted, practical way to train their hidden units.
events.idea: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed that gradient descent with errors propagated backward through the layers (the chain rule) lets hidden units learn useful internal representations.
events.changed: The paper revived connectionism in the late 1980s. Backpropagation is still used to train essentially every neural network, including LLMs.
events.limits: Earlier work derived reverse-mode differentiation (Linnainmaa 1970) and applied it to networks (Werbos 1974). Deep or recurrent nets still trained poorly because of vanishing gradients, small data and slow hardware.

links.note: trainable hidden layers escape single-layer limits
first major applied success of backprop

terms.def: Computing the gradient of a loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backward from the output layer.

verified.note: Crossref: Nature, October 1986 (issue of 9 Oct 1986). Journal paper; date_basis field reused. Nature page redirects to a login gateway for scripts but resolves in a browser. Review 2026-11-06: corrected date_basis to journal publication; the earlier source-check evidence is retained.

events.date_context: December 1989 digit-recognition paper; LeNet-5 and the consolidated document-recognition account appeared in 1998.
events.title: LeCun et al.: convolutional networks for handwritten digits (LeNet)
events.label: LeNet / ConvNets
events.problem: Fully connected nets ignore the spatial structure of images, so they need too many parameters and too much data.
events.idea: The team trained a network with local receptive fields and shared weights (convolutions) end-to-end by backprop on zip-code digits. The 1998 'Gradient-based learning' paper (LeNet-5) consolidated the design for document recognition.
events.changed: The work established convolutional networks and the idea of building domain structure into the architecture. LeNet-style systems read a sizeable share of US bank cheques in the late 1990s.
events.limits: On the hardware of the time, the design did not scale beyond small images. In the 2000s, SVMs and hand-engineered features dominated vision benchmarks.

links.note: AlexNet is a scaled-up LeNet on GPUs

terms.def: Applying the same small filter at every position of the input, so the number of parameters does not grow with image size.

verified.note: Crossref: Neural Computation Dec 1989; Proc. IEEE 1998 (November issue). Journal papers; date_basis field reused. Review 2026-11-06: corrected date_basis to journal publication; the earlier source-check evidence is retained.

events.date_context: November 1997 journal paper; the forget-gate refinement discussed in the card came later.
events.title: Long Short-Term Memory
events.label: LSTM
events.problem: Recurrent networks could not learn dependencies over more than a few time steps because gradients vanish or explode when propagated back through time (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio et al. 1994).
events.idea: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber added a memory cell with an additive self-connection (the 'constant error carousel') and multiplicative gates controlling what is written and read; a forget gate was added by Gers et al. in 2000.
events.changed: LSTMs became the default sequence model from about 2013 to 2017, powering speech recognition, seq2seq translation and ELMo.
events.limits: LSTMs still process tokens one at a time, so training cannot be parallelised across the sequence, and very long-range information still degrades. Transformers displaced them for most language work after 2017.

links.note: seq2seq used deep LSTMs as encoder and decoder
the recurrent approach the Transformer replaced

terms.def: Gradients shrinking exponentially as they are multiplied through many layers or time steps, so early inputs barely affect learning.

verified.note: Crossref: Neural Computation, Nov 1997. Journal paper; date_basis field reused. Review 2026-11-06: corrected date_basis to journal publication; the earlier source-check evidence is retained.

events.date_context: February 2003 JMLR paper; the date is a journal-publication milestone, not the origin of every neural language-modeling objective.
events.title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model
events.label: Neural language model
events.problem: Count-based n-gram models needed smoothing to handle rare or unseen word combinations, and longer contexts required rapidly growing tables. Could learned distributed representations share statistical strength across similar contexts?
events.idea: Bengio et al. jointly learned a dense vector for each word and a neural network that predicts the next word from the previous words' vectors. Similar words could then share statistical strength.
events.changed: The work helped establish jointly learned word representations and neural next-word prediction, an important ancestor of today's autoregressive language models.
events.limits: Training was far slower than for n-grams on 2003 hardware, and the model still had a fixed, short context window. N-gram models stayed dominant in production for another decade.

links.note: word2vec made the embedding part cheap and scalable

terms.def: A language model that estimates the probability of the next word from counts of the previous n-1 words.
A learned dense vector representing a word, placed so that words used in similar contexts are close together.

verified.note: JMLR page opened: Vol. 3, February 2003 issue. Journal paper; date_basis field reused. Review 2026-11-06: corrected date_basis to journal publication; the earlier source-check evidence is retained.

events.date_context: July 2006 deep-belief-network paper; the companion deep-autoencoder paper appeared the same month.
events.title: Deep belief nets and layer-wise pretraining
events.label: Deep belief nets
events.problem: Networks with many layers trained by backprop from random initialisation got stuck in poor solutions, so 'deep' networks were widely considered impractical.
events.idea: Hinton, Osindero and Teh trained a deep generative network greedily, one layer at a time, as stacked restricted Boltzmann machines, then fine-tuned the whole stack. A companion Science paper (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, Jul 2006) applied the approach to deep autoencoders.
events.changed: The work helped revive interest in training deep networks and demonstrated useful layer-wise unsupervised initialization. The pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern influenced later approaches, although the RBM recipe itself was largely displaced.
events.limits: By 2010-2012, ReLUs, better initialisation, GPUs and more labelled data made plain supervised backprop work without the specific RBM pretraining recipe.

links.note: same group, renewed belief in depth

verified.note: Crossref: Neural Computation July 2006; Science 28 Jul 2006. Journal papers; date_basis field reused. Review 2026-11-06: corrected date_basis to journal publication; the earlier source-check evidence is retained.

events.title: ImageNet: a large-scale hierarchical image database
events.label: ImageNet dataset
events.problem: Vision datasets had thousands to tens of thousands of images, too small to train high-capacity models or to separate methods convincingly.
events.idea: Deng, Fei-Fei Li and colleagues labelled millions of images over WordNet categories using crowd workers (Amazon Mechanical Turk); the yearly ILSVRC challenge (1,000 classes, about 1.2M training images) started in 2010.
events.changed: ImageNet supplied the data that made large neural nets pay off and established a shared benchmark for measuring progress. Its emphasis on data as a central ingredient carried into web-scale text corpora.
events.limits: Labels contain errors and cultural biases (the person categories were later pruned), and benchmark-chasing can reward overfitting to one test set.

verified.note: Crossref: CVPR 2009, June 2009.

events.date_context: December 2012 NIPS paper; the ImageNet competition result was announced earlier that autumn.
events.title: AlexNet: ImageNet classification with deep convolutional networks
events.label: AlexNet
events.problem: Computer vision ran on hand-designed features plus shallow classifiers, and many researchers doubted that neural nets could beat them on real images.
events.idea: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton trained a large CNN (about 60M parameters) on two GPUs with ReLUs, dropout and data augmentation, winning ILSVRC-2012 with 15.3% top-5 error against 26.2% for the runner-up.
events.changed: AlexNet's large ImageNet gain encouraged much wider use of convolutional networks and investment in deep-learning research, as computer vision shifted toward GPU-trained deep learning.
events.limits: AlexNet required large labelled datasets. The models were opaque, brittle to distribution shift and vulnerable to adversarial examples (shown in 2013).

links.note: data that made the large model trainable
deep convnets made pixel-input RL possible

terms.def: Rectified linear unit, max(0, x); its non-saturating gradient made deep nets train much faster than sigmoid or tanh units.

verified.note: Proceedings page and PDF opened; PDF states 15.3% vs 26.2% for ILSVRC-2012. Dated to the NIPS conference (Dec 2012); the competition result was announced earlier, in autumn 2012.

events.title: word2vec: efficient estimation of word representations
events.label: word2vec
events.problem: Neural language models learned good word vectors but were too expensive to train on billions of words.
events.idea: Mikolov et al. dropped the hidden layer and trained shallow models (CBOW, skip-gram) on nearby-word prediction. Their vectors showed linear analogies such as king - man + woman close to queen.
events.changed: word2vec made pretrained word vectors practical and widely used as inputs to NLP systems, accelerating transfer of representations learned from unlabeled text.
events.limits: Each word had one static vector regardless of context ('bank' has one vector). The embeddings also absorbed social biases from the corpus.

links.note: simplified the neural LM to scale it
ELMo replaced static with contextual vectors

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2013-01-16.

events.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
events.label: GANs
events.problem: Deep generative models of images needed intractable likelihoods or slow sampling procedures.
events.idea: Goodfellow et al. trained a generator against a discriminator in a two-player game: the discriminator learns to tell real from generated samples, the generator learns to fool it.
events.changed: GANs dominated image generation from about 2015 to 2020 (StyleGAN and deepfakes) and made synthetic media a policy topic.
events.limits: GAN training is unstable and prone to mode collapse. Diffusion models largely replaced GANs for image generation after 2020. GANs are not part of the LLM lineage.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2014-06-10.

events.title: Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate (attention)
events.label: Attention (Bahdanau)
events.problem: Encoder-decoder RNNs squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed-length vector, and quality fell on long sentences.
events.idea: At every output step, the decoder in Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio's model computes a learned weighting over all encoder states and reads their weighted sum (soft alignment).
events.changed: Attention became standard in neural MT (Google's GNMT in 2016). The Transformer later kept this mechanism while discarding recurrence.
events.limits: The attention mechanism still sat within a sequential RNN, so training remained slow. Later work also showed that treating attention weights as explanations is unreliable.

terms.def: A layer that computes a weighted average of a set of vectors, with weights from learned similarity between a query and each vector's key.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2014-09-01.

events.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
events.label: seq2seq
events.problem: Deep nets mapped fixed-size inputs to fixed-size outputs; tasks like translation map variable-length sequences to variable-length sequences.
events.idea: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le encoded the source with a deep LSTM into a vector and decoded the target with another LSTM, reaching 34.8 BLEU on WMT'14 English-French, competitive with phrase-based systems.
events.changed: The work showed that one end-to-end neural architecture could replace a complex statistical MT pipeline. It also framed many NLP tasks as text-in, text-out.
events.limits: The fixed-size bottleneck hurt long inputs (fixed by attention), and decoding was sequential and slow.

links.note: deep LSTMs as encoder and decoder

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2014-09-10; BLEU 34.8 from abstract.

events.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
events.label: Adam optimizer
events.problem: Plain SGD needed careful per-problem learning-rate tuning and handled badly scaled or sparse gradients poorly.
events.idea: Kingma and Ba combined momentum with per-parameter step sizes from running estimates of the first and second moments of the gradient, with bias correction.
events.changed: Adam became a widely used adaptive optimizer for deep learning. Its decoupled-weight-decay variant AdamW (2017) became common in language-model training.
events.limits: The original convergence proof was later shown to be flawed (Reddi et al. 2018), and Adam can generalise worse than SGD on some vision tasks. Its two extra state tensors add memory cost at LLM scale.

links.note: Transformer was trained with Adam plus warmup

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2014-12-22.

events.date_context: 10 December 2015 ResNet preprint; batch normalization (2015) and layer normalization (2016) are separate related developments.
events.title: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet), with batch and layer normalization
events.label: ResNet and normalization
events.problem: Beyond about 20-30 layers, adding depth made even training error worse (the degradation problem), and deep nets were slow and fragile to train.
events.idea: He et al. made each block learn a residual F(x) added to an identity shortcut, training 152-layer networks that won ILSVRC-2015. In related work, normalization layers stabilised training: batch norm (Ioffe and Szegedy, Feb 2015) for CNNs and layer norm (Ba, Kiros, Hinton, Jul 2016) for sequence models.
events.changed: Residual connections and normalization became standard ingredients of deep networks, including Transformer blocks, making much deeper stacks practical to train.
events.limits: Why residual nets work so well is still only partly understood. Batch norm depends on batch statistics, which is why Transformers use layer norm (later RMSNorm).

links.note: residual + layer norm around each sublayer

terms.def: A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, so the block only needs to learn a correction and gradients flow through the identity path.

events.date_context: 23 January 2017 sparse-MoE preprint; later examples include Switch (2021), Mixtral (2023–24) and Gemini 1.5 (2024).
events.title: Sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer
events.label: Mixture of experts
events.problem: Increasing model capacity also increased compute: every parameter was used for every token, so bigger models cost proportionally more per token.
events.idea: Shazeer et al. inserted layers of many expert sub-networks with a learned router that sends each token to only a few experts, reaching over 100B parameters at modest compute per token.
events.changed: Conditional computation became a main way to scale models. Switch Transformer (Jan 2021), Mixtral (Dec 2023/Jan 2024), Gemini 1.5 and DeepSeek-V3 use MoE; several closed frontier models are also reported to use it.
events.limits: Routing is hard to balance (auxiliary losses, dropped tokens), training can be unstable, and total memory stays large. Parameter counts of MoE and dense models are not directly comparable.

terms.def: An architecture where a router activates only a few of many expert sub-networks per token, so total parameters grow without a matching growth in compute per token.

verified.note: arXiv API: 1701.06538 v1 2017-01-23; Switch 2021-01-11; Mixtral 2024-01-08 (model announced Dec 2023, not separately verified).

events.title: Attention Is All You Need
events.label: Transformer
events.problem: RNN-based models process tokens sequentially, which limits parallel training on GPUs and makes long-range dependencies hard.
events.idea: Vaswani et al. built an encoder-decoder entirely from multi-head self-attention and feed-forward layers, with positional encodings, residual connections and layer norm. It set MT records (28.4 BLEU En-De) at lower training cost.
events.changed: The Transformer became the architecture for nearly all later language, vision and multimodal foundation models because it parallelises across the sequence and keeps improving as it is scaled.
events.limits: Self-attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. The architecture has no built-in recurrence or memory beyond the context window and requires large amounts of data and compute.

terms.def: Attention whose queries, keys and values come from the same sequence. A mask determines which positions each token may attend to; causal language models attend only to the current and earlier positions.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2017-06-12; BLEU from abstract.

events.title: ELMo: deep contextualized word representations
events.label: ELMo
events.problem: Static word vectors give a word the same representation in every sentence.
events.idea: Peters et al. took internal states of a pretrained bidirectional LSTM language model as context-dependent word features and added them to task models, improving six benchmarks.
events.changed: The results showed that a language model's internal representations transfer broadly. ELMo, together with ULMFiT (Jan 2018), opened the 2018 shift to pretrained LMs.
events.limits: Features were plugged into separate task architectures rather than fine-tuning one model, and the LSTM base was soon outscaled by Transformers.

links.note: BERT made the contextual model the task model

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2018-02-15.

events.title: GPT: Improving language understanding by generative pre-training
events.label: GPT-1
events.problem: Labelled data for each NLP task is scarce, while unlabelled text is abundant; how best to use the latter was unsettled.
events.idea: Radford et al. pretrained a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer (about 117M parameters) on BooksCorpus with next-token prediction, then fine-tuned it with minimal task-specific changes.
events.changed: GPT set the template of generative pretraining plus fine-tuning on a decoder-only Transformer, the line that leads to GPT-2, GPT-3 and ChatGPT.
events.limits: GPT still needed supervised fine-tuning per task, and BERT outperformed it on understanding benchmarks months later.

terms.def: Pretraining learns broad representations from a large corpus, using an objective such as next-token prediction or masked-token reconstruction. Post-training adapts that model for specific uses through fine-tuning, instruction tuning or preference/reward optimization.

verified.note: OpenAI page opened in a browser (curl gets 403): dated June 11, 2018. Paper has no arXiv version.

events.title: BERT: Pre-training of deep bidirectional Transformers
events.label: BERT
events.problem: Left-to-right LMs see only preceding context, which is a poor fit for understanding tasks where the whole sentence is available.
events.idea: Devlin et al. pretrained a Transformer encoder with masked-token prediction (plus next-sentence prediction), then fine-tuned it, setting state of the art on 11 tasks including GLUE and SQuAD.
events.changed: With BERT, pretrain-then-fine-tune rapidly became standard NLP practice. BERT entered Google Search (2019) and spawned many variants (RoBERTa, ALBERT).
events.limits: Encoder-only models do not generate text naturally, and the 2020s frontier shifted toward decoder-only LMs. BERT's benchmark gains partly reflected dataset artefacts.

terms.def: Pretraining by hiding a fraction of input tokens and training the model to predict them from both left and right context.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2018-10-11.

events.date_context: 14 February 2019 announcement; the full 1.5B weights were released on 5 November 2019.
events.title: GPT-2 and its staged release
events.label: GPT-2 staged release
events.problem: It was unclear how far language-model task ability would improve with larger datasets and models, and how access decisions should respond to possible misuse.
events.idea: OpenAI trained a 1.5B-parameter decoder on 40GB of web text (WebText) and showed coherent long-form generation and zero-shot ability on several tasks. Citing misuse concerns, it withheld the full model and released progressively larger versions, ending with 1.5B on 5 Nov 2019.
events.changed: GPT-2 demonstrated strong generation and zero-shot task performance from a larger pretrained LM. OpenAI's staged release became a prominent public case of restricting access over misuse concerns and intensified discussion of publication and access norms.
events.limits: GPT-2 remained unreliable on many tasks and prone to fabrication and bias. A staged release could inform an access decision, but did not by itself establish how much real-world misuse the model would cause.

sources.label: OpenAI: Better language models and their implications
OpenAI: GPT-2 1.5B release (end of staged release)

links.note: safety concerns entering lab release decisions

terms.def: Publishing successively larger versions of a model over time so that misuse and societal effects can be observed before full release.

verified.note: Both OpenAI pages opened in a browser: Feb 14, 2019 and Nov 5, 2019.

events.title: T5: exploring transfer learning with a unified text-to-text Transformer
events.label: T5
events.problem: Many pretraining objectives, architectures and datasets were proposed, each compared under different setups.
events.idea: Raffel et al. cast every task as text-to-text, ran a large controlled comparison, released the C4 web corpus and scaled an encoder-decoder to 11B parameters.
events.changed: T5 made 'every task is text in, text out' the default framing that instruction tuning (T0, FLAN-T5) built on. C4 became a standard corpus.
events.limits: Encoder-decoder models were later outpaced by decoder-only LMs for general-purpose use; C4 filtering removed some dialects and minority-group text.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2019-10-23.

events.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
events.label: Scaling laws
events.problem: Labs needed a quantitative way to trade off model size, training data and compute when planning larger language-model runs.
events.idea: Kaplan et al. found that test loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute over many orders of magnitude, with architecture details mattering little. They derived a compute-optimal allocation favouring large models trained on relatively little data.
events.changed: The paper provided empirical curves for planning and extrapolating language-model training loss, helping motivate larger runs such as GPT-3. The safety implication is a forecasting question: how does predictable average loss relate to specific capabilities and risks?
events.limits: These laws predict loss, not specific capabilities. Chinchilla revised the data-vs-parameters split, and the laws assume no data limits and a fixed recipe.

links.note: smooth loss vs abrupt task gains

terms.def: An empirical power-law relation between a model's loss and its parameter count, training data or compute.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2020-01-23.

events.title: GPT-3: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
events.label: GPT-3
events.problem: Many NLP tasks required task-specific fine-tuning; earlier zero-shot models suggested that a larger pretrained LM might adapt to more tasks through its prompt alone.
events.idea: Brown et al. trained a 175B-parameter decoder and showed it could do many tasks from an instruction and a few examples placed in the prompt, without any weight updates.
events.changed: GPT-3 made few-shot in-context learning and prompting central to general-purpose language-model use. It became a base for InstructGPT, while the API offered a way to use the model without training a task-specific system.
events.limits: Few-shot results were uneven, and the model fabricated facts, followed instructions poorly and reproduced biases from web text. Later work showed it was undertrained for its size.

links.note: InstructGPT is GPT-3 fine-tuned with RLHF
instruction tuning beat its zero-shot results

terms.def: A model performing a new task from instructions or examples in its prompt, with no change to its weights.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2020-05-28.

events.date_context: 3 September 2021 FLAN preprint; T0 followed on 15 October 2021.
events.title: Instruction tuning: FLAN and T0
events.label: Instruction tuning
events.problem: Raw pretrained LMs responded to prompts inconsistently; effective zero-shot use required careful prompt engineering.
events.idea: FLAN (Wei et al.) fine-tuned a 137B LM on 60+ NLP datasets phrased as natural-language instructions. It beat zero-shot GPT-3 on 20 of 25 unseen tasks. T0 (Sanh et al., 15 Oct 2021, BigScience) applied the approach with a multitask prompted T5.
events.changed: The results showed that supervised multitask instruction tuning can improve performance on held-out tasks. This is related to, but distinct from, the human demonstration fine-tuning used in InstructGPT and dialogue assistants.
events.limits: Academic task templates are narrow compared with real user requests, and gains depended on model scale. Instruction following alone does not make a model honest or safe.

links.note: related supervised instruction-following approach; the demonstration datasets and recipes differ
related supervised instruction-following approach; the demonstration datasets and recipes differ

terms.def: Supervised fine-tuning of a pretrained LM on many tasks phrased as instructions, so it follows new instructions zero-shot.

events.title: Chain-of-thought prompting
events.label: Chain-of-thought
events.problem: LLMs did badly on multi-step arithmetic and reasoning when asked for the answer directly.
events.idea: Wei et al. put a few worked examples with intermediate reasoning steps in the prompt; with PaLM 540B and eight such exemplars this reached state of the art on GSM8K. The gains appeared mainly in large models.
events.changed: Writing intermediate reasoning steps became a core prompting technique, leading to self-consistency, zero-shot 'let's think step by step' and eventually RL-trained reasoning models (o1, R1). Visible reasoning also became an object of safety research (CoT monitoring, faithfulness).
events.limits: Written reasoning is not necessarily the computation that produced the answer (later unfaithfulness results), and gains on small models were weak or negative.

links.note: RL to train long chains of thought

terms.def: Intermediate reasoning steps the model writes before its final answer.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2022-01-28.

events.title: Chinchilla: Training compute-optimal large language models
events.label: Chinchilla
events.problem: Following Kaplan et al., labs grew parameter counts (GPT-3 175B, Gopher 280B) while keeping training data around 300B tokens.
events.idea: Hoffmann et al. trained 400+ models and found parameters and tokens should be scaled equally (roughly 20 tokens per parameter). Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens with Gopher's compute, outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 and larger models.
events.changed: Chinchilla shifted the bottleneck from parameters to data, set the recipe for LLaMA and later models, and made high-quality training tokens a central resource.
events.limits: The allocation is compute-optimal for training alone. When inference cost matters, labs deliberately 'overtrain' smaller models far past 20 tokens per parameter. The fitted coefficients were later questioned in replication attempts.

links.note: LLaMA trained small models on many tokens

terms.def: The model size and token count that minimise loss for a fixed training compute budget.

verified.note: arXiv API: v1 2022-03-29.

events.date_context: 15 June 2022 emergence paper; the metric-based rebuttal appeared in April 2023.
events.title: Emergent abilities of LLMs, and the 'mirage' rebuttal
events.label: Emergence debate
events.problem: Loss falls smoothly with scale, yet some task scores seemed to jump from chance to well above chance at a particular model size.
events.idea: Wei et al. catalogued such 'emergent' abilities, absent in smaller models and present in larger ones. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo (28 Apr 2023) argued many jumps come from nonlinear or discontinuous metrics like exact match, and that continuous metrics show smooth improvement.
events.changed: The debate framed a forecasting question for safety: can dangerous capabilities appear suddenly and unpredictably? It encouraged continuous metrics and dedicated capability evaluations.
events.limits: The issue remains unsettled. Metric choice explains many cases, but users experience thresholds (a task is either usable or not), and abrupt gains from new post-training methods are a separate issue.

sources.label: Schaeffer et al., 'Are emergent abilities a mirage?' (arXiv)

terms.def: In this debate, a task score that appears negligible in smaller models and substantial in larger ones. Whether the apparent jump is unexpected depends on the metric, measurement resolution and extrapolation method.

verified.note: arXiv API: Wei v1 2022-06-15; Schaeffer v1 2023-04-28.

events.title: ChatGPT launch
events.label: ChatGPT
events.problem: Capable LMs were accessed through APIs and prompt engineering; the general public had no easy way to use them.
events.idea: OpenAI released a free chat interface to a GPT-3.5 model fine-tuned for dialogue with supervised data and RLHF, described as a sibling of InstructGPT.
events.changed: ChatGPT brought instruction-following language models to a broad public through an accessible dialogue interface and intensified competition and policy attention. These developments form context for later frontier-AI governance, rather than a single demonstrated cause of each policy change.
events.limits: It could hallucinate confidently and was vulnerable to jailbreaks. Preference optimization can reinforce approval-seeking and refusal patterns, so helpful conversational behavior does not establish honesty or robustness.

links.note: related instruction-following research; a direct training dependency is not established
part of the same period of growing public and policy attention; no single-cause claim
part of the same period of growing public and policy attention; no single-cause claim

verified.note: OpenAI page opened in a browser: 30 Nov 2022 (served the ru-RU locale; English URL given). The page itself does not name the base model beyond being an InstructGPT sibling; 'GPT-3.5' is from OpenAI's launch materials.

events.date_context: 24 February 2023 announcement; the preprint followed on 27 February. Later Llama releases are discussed as developments after that anchor.
events.title: LLaMA and the open-weights wave
events.label: LLaMA / open weights
events.problem: Many leading LLMs were available only through APIs, limiting outside study of their weights and low-cost adaptation.
events.idea: Meta released LLaMA (7B-65B), trained only on public data, with LLaMA-13B beating GPT-3 on most benchmarks. Its weights went to researchers under a non-commercial licence and leaked publicly within days.
events.changed: LLaMA accelerated the open-weights ecosystem: Alpaca/Vicuna fine-tunes, Llama 2 (July 2023, with commercial-use terms), and later families including Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek. It expanded outside experimentation and sharpened safety debates about releasing weights.
events.limits: Licences restricted use, so 'open source' is disputed for weights-only releases. Released weights cannot be recalled, and safety fine-tuning can be cheaply removed.

links.note: smaller models trained on more tokens
a later open-weights frontier model; not a claim that DeepSeek-V3 directly descends from LLaMA
open models made cheap preference-tuning research possible

terms.def: Publishing a trained model's parameters for download, whether or not training data and code are also released.

verified.note: Meta blog opened: 24 Feb 2023; arXiv v1 27 Feb 2023; Llama 3.1 blog 23 Jul 2024. The leak date (early March 2023) is widely reported but not checked against a primary source.

events.title: GPT-4
events.label: GPT-4
events.problem: GPT-3.5-class models failed professional-level tasks and could not take image input.
events.idea: OpenAI released a large multimodal model with text and image input, reported to score around the top 10% on a simulated bar exam. Its technical report withheld architecture, size, data and compute; a system card described pre-release red teaming.
events.changed: GPT-4 became a widely used frontier reference and an important subject of the 2023 risk debate. Its report paired limited architectural disclosure with a system card and external red teaming, making the tradeoff between capability evaluation and technical transparency especially visible.
events.limits: Its secrecy limited outside scrutiny; it still hallucinated and was jailbreakable. Benchmark contamination and the meaning of exam scores were disputed.

links.note: same post-training pipeline at larger scale
report claims loss was predicted from small runs
capability evaluation and public risk discussion in the same period; not a single-cause attribution

verified.note: OpenAI page opened in a browser: 14 Mar 2023; arXiv v1 15 Mar 2023.

events.date_context: 6 December 2023 Gemini 1.0 announcement; the long-context Gemini 1.5 result followed in February 2024.
events.title: Gemini: native multimodality, then million-token context
events.label: Gemini, multimodal, long context
events.problem: Most multimodal LLMs bolted a vision encoder onto a text model, and context windows (a few thousand to 32K tokens) limited work on long documents, code or video.
events.idea: Google DeepMind's Gemini 1.0 was trained multimodally from the start. Gemini 1.5 (15 Feb 2024), an MoE model, offered up to 1M tokens of context (10M in research tests) with near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack retrieval.
events.changed: Native multimodality and long context became standard features of frontier models. Anthropic (Claude, launched 14 Mar 2023; Claude 3 with 200K context on 4 Mar 2024) and OpenAI (GPT-4o, 13 May 2024, real-time audio and vision) competed on the same capabilities. Google became a full frontier competitor.
events.limits: Retrieval tests overstate real long-context reasoning, which degrades on harder multi-hop tasks. Gemini 1.0's launch demo video was criticised as edited.

terms.def: The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in one forward pass, covering prompt and output.

verified.note: Opened: Gemini blog 6 Dec 2023; Gemini 1.5 blog 15 Feb 2024; Claude 14 Mar 2023; Claude 3 4 Mar 2024; GPT-4o 13 May 2024 (browser). Demo-video criticism is from press reports, not re-checked.

events.title: DeepSeek-V3: frontier-level open-weights MoE
events.label: DeepSeek-V3
events.problem: Frontier performance was assumed to require the largest US labs' budgets and unrestricted access to top GPUs.
events.idea: DeepSeek released an open-weights MoE model (671B total, 37B active per token, 14.8T tokens) with multi-head latent attention, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, multi-token prediction and FP8 training. The report states 2.788M H800 GPU-hours for the full training.
events.changed: DeepSeek reported competitive benchmark performance from an open-weights MoE with an efficient training recipe. Alongside R1 a month later, DeepSeek-V3 intensified discussion of training costs, compute efficiency and the competitiveness of open models.
events.limits: The cost figure covers only the final training run, not research, ablations or hardware purchases, and was widely misquoted as total cost. Questions about distillation from other labs' outputs and censorship of politically sensitive topics followed.

links.note: part of the wider open-weights ecosystem, without claiming direct architectural descent
R1 is RL-trained from the V3 base

verified.note: Release note opened: 2024-12-26; arXiv v1 2024-12-27; GPU-hours from abstract. Market reaction date from general knowledge.

events.title: Claude 4 and the first ASL-3 deployment
events.label: Claude 4 / ASL-3
events.problem: Models were moving from chat to long autonomous coding and agent tasks, and lab safety frameworks had not yet been triggered at a higher level in practice.
events.idea: Anthropic released Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 for hours-long agentic coding, claiming 72.5% on SWE-bench Verified for Opus 4. It also made Claude Code generally available. Opus 4 shipped under ASL-3 protections from its Responsible Scaling Policy as a precaution.
events.changed: Anthropic paired a major agentic-coding release with its precautionary activation of ASL-3 protections for Opus 4, showing how its scaling policy affected deployment when a capability threshold could not be ruled out.
events.limits: ASL-3 was applied because risk could not be excluded, not because it was demonstrated. The system card's reports of blackmail-like behaviour in contrived agentic tests drew attention to how hard such evaluations are to interpret.

links.note: first ASL-3 activation under the RSP
both product lines expose extended reasoning; Anthropic's direct training dependence on o1 is not established

verified.note: Anthropic page opened: 22 May 2025; it links to the ASL-3 activation post. Blackmail-test detail from the system card, not re-opened here.

events.title: GPT-5: reasoning merged into the default model
events.label: GPT-5
events.problem: Users had to choose between fast chat models and slower reasoning models (o-series), and the product line was confusing.
events.idea: OpenAI shipped GPT-5 as a system combining a fast model, a deeper 'thinking' model and a real-time router that decides which to use. The system was available to all ChatGPT users.
events.changed: GPT-5 brought test-time reasoning to the default consumer experience, making reasoning models a standard offering rather than a specialist tier.
events.limits: Routing combines different behavior and latency profiles, so a single product label does not specify one fixed model or inference budget. Vendor benchmarks do not settle reliability on a user's particular task.

links.note: folds o-series reasoning into one system

verified.note: OpenAI page opened in a browser: 7 Aug 2025; router described on page. Reception summary from general coverage.

events.date_context: 7 April 2026 Project Glasswing announcement; this date marks the access decision, not a later model release.
events.title: Claude Mythos Preview withheld; Project Glasswing
events.label: Mythos Preview withheld
events.problem: Frontier models had become strong at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, which helps defenders and attackers alike.
events.idea: Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, saying it does not plan to make the frontier model generally available. It gave access only to a coalition of major software and security organisations (Project Glasswing) to find and fix vulnerabilities in critical software.
events.changed: Anthropic restricted model access on misuse grounds, organizing the decision around defensive cybersecurity work. The decision raised questions about who can access powerful vulnerability-discovery systems and how the effects of restricted access can be measured.
events.limits: Capability claims come mostly from Anthropic and partners; the long-run effect on vulnerability balance is unknown. Restricted access concentrates powerful capabilities in a few large firms.

links.note: next step in the Claude line

verified.note: Glasswing page opened: dated 7 Apr 2026, states the model will not be made generally available; page has an Oct 2026 update. Mythos/Fable 5.1 date seen on the Anthropic news index (15 Sep 2026); a third-party source gave 1 Sep, so treat as approximate.

events.title: GPT-6 Astra
events.label: GPT-6
events.problem: By 2026, frontier labs were competing more on long-horizon agentic work (computer use, software engineering, science workflows) than on chat quality.
events.idea: OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, starting with limited organisations and then paid ChatGPT plans and the API, presenting it as combining pretraining, RL and alignment advances. It reported near-ceiling scores on several hard benchmarks, including cybersecurity ones. GPT-6 Sol and Luna followed on 22 Sep 2026.
events.changed: The release is too recent to assess. It belongs to a cluster of frontier releases in September-October 2026, including Claude Opus 5.5 on 22 Sep 2026. Across these releases, saturating benchmarks and agentic, cyber-relevant capabilities dominate both marketing and safety evaluation.
events.limits: All figures are vendor-reported, several benchmarks are new or near saturation, and the page gives no technical detail on architecture or training.

links.note: cyber capability as a frontier axis

verified.note: GPT-6 Astra page opened in a browser; no visible date, but page metadata contains 2026-09-03 and press coverage agrees. Sol/Luna date from the page's own update note. Opus 5.5 page opened: 22 Sep 2026.

eras.title: Symbolic AI and the first winter
eras.summary: AI is founded at Dartmouth around logic, search and hand-written rules, with perceptrons as a side branch. Over-promising, the limits of single-layer nets and the Lighthill report bring funding cuts in the 1970s.

eras.title: Expert systems, connectionist revival, second winter
eras.summary: Commercial expert systems boom and then collapse in the late 1980s. In parallel, backpropagation revives neural networks and yields CNNs and early RNNs. Temporal-difference RL is also formalised.

eras.title: Statistical machine learning
eras.summary: Probabilistic models, SVMs, kernel methods and n-gram language models dominate, judged on shared benchmarks. Neural nets persist at the margins (LSTM, LeNet, deep belief nets) and large datasets like ImageNet appear.

eras.title: Deep learning breakthrough
eras.summary: AlexNet helped accelerate adoption of GPU-trained deep networks in vision; speech and translation followed their own overlapping neural-network trajectories. Deep RL systems such as DQN and AlphaGo combined learned representations with control and search, while earlier AI-safety concerns developed into new technical research agendas.

eras.title: Transformers and scaling
eras.summary: Transformers and large-scale self-supervised pretraining reshaped NLP through different objectives, including GPT-style causal modeling and BERT-style masking. Scaling laws made training loss easier to forecast. GPT-3 brought in-context learning to wider attention, while alignment research expanded alongside capability work.

eras.title: Assistants and RLHF
eras.summary: Instruction tuning and RLHF turn pretrained LMs into assistants, and ChatGPT makes them a mass product. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini and open-weights LLaMA make these capabilities more widely available. Governments respond with summits, statements and the EU AI Act.

eras.title: Reasoning models and agents
eras.summary: RL on chains of thought (o1, R1) gives test-time reasoning, and models are deployed as long-running coding and computer-use agents. Lab safety frameworks are triggered in practice and some frontier models are withheld or released only to restricted groups.

threads.title: How did neural networks come back?
threads.question: Neural nets were written off twice; what changed between 1969 and 2012?
threads.summary: Perceptron limitations and the funding downturn formed part of the background to neural networks' later revival; the book alone did not determine that history. Backpropagation made hidden-layer learning practical, while CNNs and LSTMs provided structures suited to images and sequences. Unsupervised layer-wise pretraining showed that deeper networks could be trained before large labeled datasets and GPUs helped AlexNet achieve a decisive vision result. Residual connections and normalization then made very deep networks easier to train.

threads.title: Why did transformers win?
threads.question: What problems of earlier sequence models did the Transformer solve, and why did it generalise beyond translation?
threads.summary: Neural LMs and word2vec made distributed representations useful for language, while seq2seq offered end-to-end translation. Recurrent processing limited parallelism, and fixed-vector encoders created a bottleneck. Attention supplied content-dependent access to encoder states; the Transformer combined attention and feed-forward blocks without recurrence, enabling sequence-parallel training. GPT, BERT and T5 then used different architectures and pretraining objectives rather than one universal next-token recipe.

threads.title: What does scale buy, and what not?
threads.question: How predictable are the gains from more compute, data and parameters, and where does the prediction break down?
threads.summary: GPT-2 and GPT-3 demonstrated broad text generation and task performance in larger autoregressive LMs. Scaling laws related average loss to parameters, data and compute; Chinchilla revised their compute-optimal allocation. MoE and efficient open models offered other ways to spend compute. Smooth loss trends still do not directly predict every capability, factual reliability or alignment. Post-training and inference-time reasoning added further sources of improvement, whose contribution varies by system and task.

threads.title: How did a pretrained LM become an assistant?
threads.question: What steps turned a text predictor into a model that follows instructions and holds a conversation?
threads.summary: GPT-3 could adapt through prompting, but raw pretraining did not reliably produce an instruction-following assistant. Multitask instruction tuning and demonstration fine-tuning improved that behavior; rewards learned from preferences and RLHF added human-rated objectives. ChatGPT brought dialogue assistants to broad use. Chain-of-thought prompting and RL-trained reasoning offered stronger multi-step problem solving, and systems that paired assistants with tools turned them into agents. Gains in helpfulness do not automatically establish honesty or robustness.
